mcqs.question: A 35-year-old has HBV DNA >2000 IU/ml and ALT of 45 IU/L on 2 tests 3 months apart. What does NICE recommend?
mcqs.explanation: NICE offers antivirals to adults aged 30 or over with HBV DNA >2000 IU/ml and abnormal ALT (≥30 men, ≥19 women) on 2 tests 3 months apart.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer antiviral treatment to adults aged 30 years and older who have HBV DNA greater than 2000 IU/ml and abnormal ALT (greater than or equal to 30 IU/L in males and greater than or equal to 19 IU/L in females) on 2 consecutive tests conducted 3 months apart.

mcqs.question: What ALT thresholds does NICE use to define abnormal ALT in hepatitis B?
mcqs.explanation: NICE defines abnormal ALT as 30 IU/L or more in males and 19 IU/L or more in females.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer antiviral treatment to adults aged 30 years and older who have HBV DNA greater than 2000 IU/ml and abnormal ALT (greater than or equal to 30 IU/L in males and greater than or equal to 19 IU/L in females) on 2 consecutive tests conducted 3 months apart.

Monitor ALT and HBV DNA levels every 48 weeks in adults with inactive chronic hepatitis B infection (defined as HBeAg negative on 2 consecutive tests with normal ALT [less than 30 IU/L in males and less than 19 IU/L in females] and HBV DNA less than 2000 IU/ml).

mcqs.question: An adult has cirrhosis and detectable HBV DNA. When does NICE offer antivirals?

options.C: Regardless of HBeAg, DNA or ALT

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Regardless of HBeAg, DNA or ALT
mcqs.explanation: Offer antivirals to adults with cirrhosis and detectable HBV DNA regardless of HBeAg status, HBV DNA level or ALT.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer antiviral treatment to adults with cirrhosis and detectable HBV DNA, regardless of HBeAg status, HBV DNA and ALT levels.

mcqs.question: How often does NICE recommend monitoring ALT and HBV DNA in inactive chronic hepatitis B?
mcqs.explanation: Monitor ALT and HBV DNA every 48 weeks in inactive chronic HBV.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Monitor ALT and HBV DNA levels every 48 weeks in adults with inactive chronic hepatitis B infection (defined as HBeAg negative on 2 consecutive tests with normal ALT [less than 30 IU/L in males and less than 19 IU/L in females] and HBV DNA less than 2000 IU/ml).

mcqs.question: A pregnant woman has HBV DNA >10⁷ IU/ml. What does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: Offer tenofovir disoproxil in the third trimester to women with HBV DNA >10⁷ IU/ml to reduce transmission.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer tenofovir disoproxil to women with HBV DNA greater than 10 7 IU/ml in the third trimester to reduce the risk of transmission of HBV to the baby. In June 2013, this was an off-label use of tenofovir disoproxil. See NICE's information on prescribing medicines .

mcqs.question: Within what timeframe should HBsAg-positive pregnant women be referred for specialist assessment, according to NICE?
mcqs.explanation: Refer within 6 weeks of the screening result so treatment can be given in the third trimester.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Refer pregnant women who are HBsAg positive to a hepatologist, or to a gastroenterologist or infectious disease specialist with an interest in hepatology, for assessment within 6 weeks of receiving the screening test result and to allow treatment in the third trimester (see recommendation 1.5.35 in the section on women who are pregnant or breastfeeding ).

mcqs.question: An HBsAg-positive person with HBV DNA >2000 IU/ml is starting immunosuppression. Which prophylaxis does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: Offer prophylaxis with entecavir or tenofovir disoproxil when HBsAg positive with HBV DNA >2000 IU/ml.

sourceRefs.excerpt: In people who are HBsAg positive and have HBV DNA greater than 2000 IU/ml, offer prophylaxis with entecavir or tenofovir disoproxil.

mcqs.question: HBV DNA is <2000 IU/ml and immunosuppression is expected to last <6 months. Which prophylaxis does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: Consider lamivudine, switching to tenofovir if HBV DNA remains detectable after 6 months.

sourceRefs.excerpt: consider lamivudine in people with HBV DNA less than 2000 IU/ml and for whom immunosuppressive therapy is expected to last less than 6 months; change to tenofovir disoproxil if HBV DNA remains detectable after 6 months

mcqs.question: When does NICE say HBV prophylaxis should start and stop around immunosuppression?

options.C: After the first cycle; stop at end

mcqs.explanation: Start prophylaxis before immunosuppressive therapy and continue for at least 6 months after HBeAg seroconversion with undetectable HBV DNA.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Start prophylaxis before beginning immunosuppressive therapy and continue for a minimum of 6 months after HBeAg seroconversion and HBV DNA is undetectable.

mcqs.question: Who does NICE say should NOT be offered prophylaxis?

options.C: HBsAg-positive with HBV DNA below 2000 IU/ml
options.D: HBsAg-positive with HBV DNA above 2000 IU/ml
options.E: Anyone on other B-cell depleting therapy

mcqs.explanation: People who are HBsAg negative, anti-HBc and anti-HBs positive, and not on rituximab or other B-cell depleting therapies shouldn't be offered prophylaxis.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer prophylaxis to people who are HBsAg negative and anti-HBc and anti-HBs positive who are not taking rituximab or other B cell-depleting therapies.

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about genotype testing to choose initial treatment for chronic hepatitis B?
mcqs.explanation: NICE says not to offer genotype testing to determine initial treatment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer genotype testing to determine initial treatment in people with chronic hepatitis B.

mcqs.question: Which drug does NICE say should NOT be offered for chronic hepatitis B?
mcqs.explanation: NICE advises against offering adefovir dipivoxil for chronic hepatitis B.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer adefovir dipivoxil for treatment of chronic hepatitis B.

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about peginterferon alfa-2a in decompensated liver disease?
mcqs.explanation: NICE says not to offer peginterferon alfa-2a to people with decompensated liver disease.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer peginterferon alfa-2a to people with chronic hepatitis B and decompensated liver disease.

mcqs.question: At 24 weeks of peginterferon, HBV DNA has fallen by <2 log₁₀ IU/ml. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: Consider stopping peginterferon at 24 weeks if DNA has fallen by <2 log or HBsAg is >20,000 IU/ml, and offer second-line treatment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider stopping peginterferon alfa-2a 24 weeks after starting treatment if HBV DNA level has decreased by less than 2 log 10 IU/ml and/or if HBsAg is greater than 20,000 IU/ml, and offer second-line treatment in line with recommendations 1.5.14 and 1.5.15.

mcqs.question: HBV DNA is still detectable at 48 weeks of tenofovir. What does NICE suggest as third-line treatment?
mcqs.explanation: Consider switching between tenofovir and entecavir as third-line treatment when HBV DNA is detectable at 48 weeks.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider switching from tenofovir disoproxil to entecavir, or from entecavir to tenofovir disoproxil, as third-line treatment in people who have detectable HBV DNA at 48 weeks of treatment.

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest considering stopping nucleos(t)ide treatment in a patient without cirrhosis?
mcqs.explanation: Consider stopping 12 months after achieving undetectable HBV DNA and HBsAg seroconversion (or HBeAg seroconversion) in people without cirrhosis.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider stopping nucleoside or nucleotide analogue treatment 12 months after achieving undetectable HBV DNA and HBsAg seroconversion in people without cirrhosis.
Consider stopping nucleoside or nucleotide analogue treatment 12 months after HBeAg seroconversion in people without cirrhosis.

mcqs.question: When does NICE schedule HBV DNA, quantitative HBsAg and HBeAg monitoring after starting tenofovir?

options.B: Baseline and then once yearly only
options.D: Every 2 years after the baseline test
options.E: Only once, at week 48 of treatment

mcqs.explanation: Monitor before starting, at 12, 24 and 48 weeks, then every 6 months.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Monitor HBV DNA and quantitative HBsAg levels and HBeAg status before starting tenofovir disoproxil, 12, 24 and 48 weeks after starting treatment and then every 6 months to determine treatment response and medicines adherence.

mcqs.question: After HBsAg seroconversion on treatment, when does NICE suggest discharge?

options.B: After a single negative HBsAg test

mcqs.explanation: Monitor HBsAg and anti-HBs annually and discharge once anti-HBs is positive on 2 consecutive tests.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Monitor HBsAg and anti-HBs annually in people with HBsAg seroconversion after antiviral treatment and discharge people who are anti-HBs positive on 2 consecutive tests.

mcqs.question: Which treatment does NICE offer for adults co-infected with chronic hepatitis B and C?
mcqs.explanation: Offer peginterferon alfa and ribavirin to adults co-infected with chronic hepatitis B and C.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer peginterferon alfa and ribavirin in adults co-infected with chronic hepatitis B and C. Avoid use of peginterferon alfa-2a in pregnancy unless the potential benefit outweighs risk. Women of childbearing potential must use effective contraception throughout therapy.

mcqs.question: According to EASL 2018, what is now the commonest cause of acute viral hepatitis in many European countries?
mcqs.explanation: Locally acquired (zoonotic) HEV is now the commonest cause of acute viral hepatitis in many European countries.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Given that locally acquired HEV is now the commonest cause of acute viral hepatitis in many European countries, understanding the paradigm shift in zoonotic HEV and its global health implications is crucial.

topics.coverageNote: Pool covers pancreatic cancer, PDAC and pancreatic cysts. Mostly NICE NG85 rows, which are stored with sourceYear 2001 (a data error: NG85 is a 2018 guideline). Also includes trials from 2015–2022 (ESPAC-4, PRODIGE, PREOPANC), ESGE 2017, ISGPS 2014 and REDISCOVER 2024. A few chronic or acute pancreatitis rows were excluded.

mcqs.question: A patient with newly diagnosed pancreatic cancer hasn't had a pancreatic protocol CT. What does NICE offer?

options.D: PET-CT as the only staging test

mcqs.explanation: Offer a pancreatic protocol CT that includes the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For people with newly diagnosed pancreatic cancer who have not had a pancreatic protocol CT scan, offer a pancreatic protocol CT scan that includes the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

mcqs.question: A patient has obstructive jaundice and suspected pancreatic cancer. What does NICE say should happen before biliary drainage?
mcqs.explanation: Offer a pancreatic protocol CT scan before draining the bile duct.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For people with obstructive jaundice and suspected pancreatic cancer, offer a pancreatic protocol CT scan before draining the bile duct.

mcqs.question: What does ESGE 2017 recommend first-line for solid pancreatic lesions when a pathological diagnosis is required?
mcqs.explanation: ESGE recommends EUS-guided sampling as the first-line procedure.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For pancreatic solid lesions, ESGE recommends performing endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided sampling as first-line procedure when a pathological diagnosis is required.

mcqs.question: Which adjuvant regimen does NICE offer after pancreatic cancer resection?
mcqs.explanation: Offer adjuvant gemcitabine plus capecitabine once the patient has recovered after resection (off-label in February 2018).

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer adjuvant gemcitabine plus capecitabine to people who have had sufficient time to recover after pancreatic cancer resection. In February 2018, this was an off-label use. See NICE's information on prescribing medicines .

mcqs.question: Which regimen did the 2018 PRODIGE trial compare with gemcitabine as adjuvant therapy in resected PDAC?
mcqs.explanation: The trial randomised 493 patients with resected PDAC to modified FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine.

sourceRefs.excerpt: We compared the efficacy and safety of a modified FOLFIRINOX regimen with gemcitabine as adjuvant therapy in patients with resected pancreatic cancer. Methods We randomly assigned 493 patients with resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma to receive a modified FOLFIRINOX regimen (oxaliplatin [85 mg per square meter of body-surface area], irinotecan [180 mg per square meter, reduced to 150

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about neoadjuvant therapy for borderline resectable pancreatic cancer?
mcqs.explanation: Only consider neoadjuvant therapy for borderline resectable disease as part of a clinical trial.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Only consider neoadjuvant therapy for people with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer as part of a clinical trial.

mcqs.question: Metastatic pancreatic cancer with ECOG 0–1: what does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: Offer FOLFIRINOX to people with metastatic pancreatic cancer and ECOG performance status 0–1.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer FOLFIRINOX to people with metastatic pancreatic cancer and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 to 1. In February 2018, this was an off-label use. See NICE's information on prescribing medicines .

mcqs.question: A patient with metastatic pancreatic cancer can't tolerate FOLFIRINOX. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: Consider gemcitabine combination therapy. Nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine is a TA option.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider gemcitabine combination therapy for people who are not well enough to tolerate FOLFIRINOX. Paclitaxel as albumin-bound nanoparticles (nab-paclitaxel) with gemcitabine is recommended as an option in NICE technology appraisal guidance for untreated metastatic adenocarcinoma of the pancreas if other combination chemotherapies are unsuitable and people would otherwise have gemcitabine monotherapy. For full details, see the guidance on nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine (TA476, 2017) . In Septe

mcqs.question: Locally advanced pancreatic cancer in a patient fit for treatment: what does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: Offer systemic combination chemotherapy if well enough. Consider gemcitabine if not well enough for combination therapy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer systemic combination chemotherapy to people with locally advanced pancreatic cancer who are well enough to tolerate it.
Consider gemcitabine for people with locally advanced pancreatic cancer who are not well enough to tolerate combination chemotherapy.

mcqs.question: For unresectable pancreatic cancer with biliary obstruction, what does NICE recommend instead of surgical biliary bypass?
mcqs.explanation: Offer endoscopically placed self-expanding metal stents rather than surgical bypass.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer endoscopically placed self-expanding metal stents rather than surgical biliary bypass to people with unresectable pancreatic cancer.

mcqs.question: A head of pancreas cancer is found to be unresectable during attempted resection. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: Consider prophylactic gastrojejunostomy and surgical biliary bypass if the cancer is found to be unresectable.

sourceRefs.excerpt: During attempted resection for head of pancreas cancer, consider prophylactic gastrojejunostomy if the cancer is found to be unresectable.
During attempted resection for pancreatic cancer, consider surgical biliary bypass if the cancer is found to be unresectable.

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about fish oils for weight loss in unresectable pancreatic cancer?
mcqs.explanation: Don't offer fish oils as a nutritional intervention to manage weight loss in unresectable pancreatic cancer.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer fish oils as a nutritional intervention to manage weight loss in people with unresectable pancreatic cancer.

mcqs.question: What does NICE suggest around pancreatic cancer resection to support digestion?
mcqs.explanation: Consider enteric-coated pancreatin before and after resection.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider enteric-coated pancreatin before and after pancreatic cancer resection.

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest an EUS- or image-guided coeliac plexus block?
mcqs.explanation: Consider a neurolytic coeliac plexus block for uncontrolled pain, unacceptable opioid adverse effects or escalating opioid doses.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider EUS-guided or image-guided percutaneous neurolytic coeliac plexus block to manage pain for people with pancreatic cancer who: have uncontrolled pancreatic pain or are experiencing unacceptable opioid adverse effects or are receiving escalating doses of analgesics.

mcqs.question: Which procedure does NICE say should NOT be offered to people with pancreatic cancer?
mcqs.explanation: NICE says not to offer thoracic splanchnicectomy to people with pancreatic cancer.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer thoracic splanchnicectomy to people with pancreatic cancer.

mcqs.question: Which group does NICE offer pancreatic cancer surveillance?
mcqs.explanation: Surveillance is offered to people with hereditary pancreatitis and a PRSS1 mutation, certain BRCA/PALB2/CDKN2A carriers with an affected relative, and other listed groups.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer surveillance for pancreatic cancer to people who meet any of the following criteria: hereditary pancreatitis and a PRSS1 mutation; BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2 or CDKN2A (p16) mutations, and 1 or more first-degree relatives with pancreatic cancer; Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about EUS to detect pancreatic cancer in people with hereditary pancreatitis?
mcqs.explanation: Don't offer EUS for detection in hereditary pancreatitis. Consider pancreatic protocol CT if there is a PRSS1 mutation.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer EUS to detect pancreatic cancer in people with hereditary pancreatitis.
Consider a pancreatic protocol CT scan for pancreatic cancer surveillance in people with hereditary pancreatitis and a PRSS1 mutation.

mcqs.question: What imaging does NICE offer for people with pancreatic cysts?
mcqs.explanation: Offer a pancreatic protocol CT or MRI/MRCP for pancreatic cysts, adding the other test if more information is needed.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer a pancreatic protocol CT scan or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRI/MRCP) to people with pancreatic cysts.
If more information is needed after either a pancreatic protocol CT scan or MRI/MRCP, offer the person whichever of these tests was not done.

mcqs.question: What do the REDISCOVER 2024 guidelines prioritise as the main indication for resection in borderline or locally advanced PDAC?
mcqs.explanation: REDISCOVER prioritises tumour biology over anatomical features as the primary indication for resection.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The REDISCOVER guidelines prioritize tumor biology over anatomical features as the primary indication for resection in borderline-resectable (BR-PDAC) and locally advanced ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreas (LA-PDAC).

mcqs.question: EUS sampling of a solid pancreatic lesion is inconclusive but suspicion remains high. What does ESGE 2017 suggest?
mcqs.explanation: ESGE suggests re-evaluating pathology slides, repeating EUS-guided sampling, or surgery.

sourceRefs.excerpt: In the case of negative or inconclusive results from EUS-guided sampling of pancreatic solid lesions and a high degree of suspicion of malignant disease, ESGE suggests re-evaluating the pathology slides, repeating EUS-guided sampling, or surgery.

topics.coverageNote: WARNING: the topic is labelled constipation, but the pool is almost entirely NICE NG123 pelvic floor dysfunction, prolapse and urinary incontinence recommendations (2006/2019 tags, no stored sourceYear). There are only 3 constipation-specific rows (JGH 2022, Saudi Med J 2023, RBGO 2022). Questions mainly test pelvic floor management. Key missing source: NICE CKS constipation or any constipation guideline.

mcqs.question: A woman has stress urinary incontinence. What first-line treatment does NICE offer?

options.A: Vaginal cones used alone at home
options.C: Pad tests and observation for 6 months

mcqs.explanation: NICE offers a trial of supervised pelvic floor muscle training of at least 3 months as first-line for stress or mixed urinary incontinence.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer a trial of supervised pelvic floor muscle training of at least 3 months' duration as first-line treatment to women with stress or mixed urinary incontinence. [2019]
Offer a programme of supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months to women (including pregnant women) with stress urinary incontinence or mixed urinary incontinence.

mcqs.question: What does NICE say a pelvic floor muscle training programme should include at minimum?
mcqs.explanation: PFMT programmes should comprise at least 8 contractions performed 3 times per day.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Pelvic floor muscle training programmes should comprise at least 8 contractions performed 3 times per day. [2006]

mcqs.question: Who should supervise pelvic floor muscle training, according to NICE?

options.A: Any healthcare assistant on the ward
options.B: The patient alone using a phone app

mcqs.explanation: PFMT should be supervised by a physiotherapist or other healthcare professional with appropriate expertise.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Pelvic floor muscle training programmes should be supervised by a physiotherapist or other healthcare professional with the appropriate expertise in pelvic floor muscle training.

mcqs.question: A woman can't perform an effective pelvic floor contraction. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: Consider supplementing PFMT with biofeedback, electrical stimulation or vaginal cones.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For women who are unable to perform an effective pelvic floor muscle contraction, consider supplementing pelvic floor muscle training with biofeedback techniques, electrical stimulation or vaginal cones.
Electrical stimulation and/or biofeedback should be considered for women who cannot actively contract pelvic floor muscles to aid motivation and adherence to therapy. [2006]

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about routinely combining electrical stimulation with PFMT?
mcqs.explanation: Electrical stimulation should not routinely be combined with PFMT.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not routinely use electrical stimulation in combination with pelvic floor muscle training. [2006]

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about vaginal diazepam for pelvic floor dysfunction?
mcqs.explanation: NICE says not to offer vaginal diazepam, even for women with high muscle tone.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer vaginal diazepam to treat pelvic floor dysfunction, even for women with high muscle tone.

mcqs.question: A woman with symptomatic POP-Q stage 2 prolapse asks about first options. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: Consider supervised PFMT for at least 16 weeks as a first option for symptomatic stage 1 or 2 prolapse.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider a programme of supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 16 weeks as a first option for women with symptomatic POP‑Q (Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification) stage 1 or stage 2 pelvic organ prolapse. If the programme is beneficial, advise women to continue pelvic floor muscle training afterwards. [2019]

mcqs.question: What does NICE suggest considering for symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse, alone or with PFMT?
mcqs.explanation: Consider a vaginal pessary for symptomatic prolapse, alone or with supervised PFMT.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider a vaginal pessary for women with symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse, alone or in conjunction with supervised pelvic floor muscle training. [2019]
Consider pessaries for women who have symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse.

mcqs.question: A woman with prolapse has a BMI of 34. What does NICE say about weight loss?

options.A: Weight has no bearing on prolapse
options.B: Advise gaining weight to support organs
options.C: Advise it; don't delay other care
options.D: Delay all treatment until weight is lost

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Advise it; don't delay other care
mcqs.explanation: Advise weight loss if BMI is over 30, but don't wait for weight loss before starting other management.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider giving advice on lifestyle to women with pelvic organ prolapse, including information on: losing weight, if the woman has a BMI greater than 30 kg/m 2; minimising heavy lifting; preventing or treating constipation. [2019]
Do not wait for women to lose weight before starting other pelvic floor dysfunction management options.

mcqs.question: Which of these lifestyle advice areas does NICE list for women with pelvic organ prolapse?
mcqs.explanation: Lifestyle advice covers losing weight if BMI >30, minimising heavy lifting, and preventing or treating constipation.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider giving advice on lifestyle to women with pelvic organ prolapse, including information on: losing weight, if the woman has a BMI greater than 30 kg/m 2; minimising heavy lifting; preventing or treating constipation. [2019]

mcqs.question: How long should supervised PFMT be offered for faecal incontinence with coexisting prolapse, according to NICE?
mcqs.explanation: Consider supervised PFMT for at least 4 months for faecal incontinence with coexisting prolapse.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider a programme of supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 4 months for women with faecal incontinence and coexisting pelvic organ prolapse.

mcqs.question: When does NICE say a 6-month review after prolapse surgery should take place, and what must it include?
mcqs.explanation: Offer a review 6 months after prolapse surgery, including vaginal examination and a check for mesh exposure if mesh was used.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer women a review 6 months after surgery for pelvic organ prolapse. Ensure that the review includes a vaginal examination and, if mesh was used, check for mesh exposure. [2019]

mcqs.question: Which pregnant women does NICE suggest a 3-month supervised PFMT programme for, starting from week 20?

options.B: Only women with a BMI under 20

mcqs.explanation: Consider a 3-month PFMT programme from week 20 for pregnant women with a first-degree relative with pelvic floor dysfunction.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider a 3‑month programme of supervised pelvic floor muscle training : from week 20 of pregnancy, for pregnant women who have a first-degree relative with pelvic floor dysfunction; during postnatal care, for women who have experienced any of the following risk factors during birth: assisted vaginal birth (forceps or vacuum); a vaginal birth when the baby is lying face up (occipito-posterior); injury to the anal sphincter.

mcqs.question: Who does NICE say should discuss pelvic floor dysfunction with women at each postnatal contact?
mcqs.explanation: Health visitors, midwives and GPs should discuss pelvic floor dysfunction at each postnatal contact.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Health visitors, midwives and GPs should discuss pelvic floor dysfunction with women at each postnatal contact.

mcqs.question: A woman with prolapse has menopausal genitourinary symptoms and a cognitive impairment that makes creams hard to use. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: Consider an oestrogen-releasing ring when cognitive or physical impairment makes pessaries or creams difficult.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider an oestrogen-releasing ring for women with pelvic organ prolapse and genitourinary symptoms and signs associated with menopause who have cognitive or physical impairments that might make vaginal oestrogen pessaries or creams difficult to use. [2019]

mcqs.question: A woman has urinary urgency and frequency. What does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: Offer supported bladder retraining, combined with other interventions such as PFMT.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer supported bladder retraining (combined with other interventions, such as pelvic floor muscle training) to women with urinary frequency, urgency or mixed incontinence.

mcqs.question: When does NICE say a regional complex pelvic floor MDT should review the proposed treatment?

options.C: All referrals made from primary care

mcqs.explanation: Regional MDTs should review proposed treatment for repeat continence surgery or repeat same-site prolapse surgery, among other cases.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Regional MDTs that deal with complex pelvic floor dysfunction and mesh-related problems should review the proposed treatment for women if: they are having repeat continence surgery; they are having repeat, same-site prolapse surgery; their preferred treatment option is not available in the referring hospital; they have coexisting bowel problems that may need additional colorectal intervention; vaginal mesh for prolapse is a treatment option for them; they have mesh complications or unexplained s

mcqs.question: A woman with anterior prolapse and stress incontinence is planning surgery. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: Consider concurrent surgery for SUI and prolapse in women with anterior and/or apical prolapse and SUI.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider concurrent surgery for stress urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women with anterior and/or apical prolapse and stress urinary incontinence. [2019]

mcqs.question: What does the 2023 Saudi Medical Journal source advise when evaluating patients with constipation?

options.C: Exclude thyroid disease and nothing else
options.D: Refer all patients for surgical review

mcqs.explanation: Clinicians should consider underlying pelvic floor disorders when evaluating constipation.

sourceRefs.excerpt: When evaluating patients with constipation, clinicians should consider the possibility of underlying pelvic floor disorders, especially in regions with a high prevalence of risk factors for PFDs.

mcqs.question: According to JGH 2022, which patient group has a high prevalence of GI symptoms including constipation?
mcqs.explanation: Gastroenterologists should be aware of the high prevalence of GI symptoms, including constipation, in hEDS and hypermobility spectrum disorders.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Gastroenterologists should be aware of the high prevalence of gastrointestinal symptoms, including constipation, in patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) and hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD).

topics.coverageNote: Mostly NICE NG78 cystic fibrosis recommendations (no stored sourceYear; covers all ages, not only adults), plus a few non-CF bronchiectasis rows from 2014–2025 that were excluded or used sparingly. Current.

mcqs.question: Who does NICE say should lead the specialist cystic fibrosis MDT?
mcqs.explanation: The specialist CF MDT should be led by a specialist paediatrician or adult physician.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The specialist cystic fibrosis multidisciplinary team should be led by a specialist paediatrician or adult physician.

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about inhaled corticosteroids as immunomodulatory treatment in CF?
mcqs.explanation: Don't offer inhaled corticosteroids as an immunomodulatory treatment for cystic fibrosis.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer inhaled corticosteroids as an immunomodulatory treatment for cystic fibrosis.

mcqs.question: A patient with CF has deteriorating lung function and repeated exacerbations. What long-term treatment does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: Offer long-term azithromycin at an immunomodulatory dose (off-label in October 2017).

sourceRefs.excerpt: For people with cystic fibrosis and deteriorating lung function or repeated pulmonary exacerbations, offer long-term treatment with azithromycin at an immunomodulatory dose . October 2017: note that this was an off-label use. See NICE's information on prescribing medicines .

mcqs.question: What respiratory prophylaxis does NICE offer children with CF from diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Offer flucloxacillin prophylaxis against S. aureus from diagnosis up to age 3, considering continuing to age 6.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer flucloxacillin as antibiotic prophylaxis against respiratory Staphylococcus aureus infection for children with cystic fibrosis from the point of diagnosis up to age 3, and consider continuing up to 6 years of age. Before starting flucloxacillin, discuss the uncertainties and possible adverse effects with their parents or carers (as appropriate). mcqs.question: A patient with CF has clinical evidence of lung disease. What does NICE offer?
mcqs.explanation: Offer a mucoactive agent to people with CF who have clinical evidence of lung disease.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer a mucoactive agent to people with cystic fibrosis who have clinical evidence of lung disease.

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about high-frequency chest wall oscillation for airway clearance in CF?

options.B: Offer it in place of technique training
options.D: Offer it routinely to all children
options.E: Offer it as first-line for everyone

mcqs.explanation: Don't offer high-frequency chest wall oscillation except in exceptional circumstances decided by the specialist team.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer high-frequency chest wall oscillation as an airway clearance technique for people with cystic fibrosis except in exceptional clinical circumstances. The specialist cystic fibrosis team will decide whether these circumstances apply, and their decision would then be subject to the NHS England policy on Individual Funding Requests . Be aware that the evidence shows high-frequency chest wall oscillation is not as effective as other airway clearance techniques.

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest non-invasive ventilation in CF?
mcqs.explanation: Consider NIV for moderate or severe lung disease when standard airway clearance techniques can't clear the lungs.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider using non-invasive ventilation in people with cystic fibrosis who have moderate or severe lung disease and cannot clear their lungs using standard airway clearance techniques.

mcqs.question: A patient with CF has H. influenzae in a respiratory culture but no clinical pulmonary infection. What does NICE advise?
mcqs.explanation: Treat with an appropriate oral antibiotic.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For people with cystic fibrosis who develop a Haemophilus influenzae infection (diagnosed by a positive respiratory sample culture) but do not have clinical evidence of pulmonary infection, treat with an appropriate oral antibiotic.

mcqs.question: A patient with CF has chronic Aspergillus infection and stable lungs. What does NICE say about suppressive antifungals?

options.E: Use them before every clinic visit

mcqs.explanation: Don't routinely use antifungals to suppress chronic Aspergillus fumigatus infection when pulmonary status is stable.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not routinely use antifungal agents to suppress chronic Aspergillus fumigatus complex respiratory infection (diagnosed by persistently positive respiratory secretion sample cultures) in people with cystic fibrosis and stable pulmonary status.

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest NTM eradication therapy in CF?

options.A: After a single positive NTM culture
options.B: Never; NTM is a commensal in CF

mcqs.explanation: Consider eradication when secretions persistently test NTM positive and the patient is clinically unwell with pulmonary disease, or CT is consistent and disease isn't responding to other treatment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider non-tuberculous mycobacterial therapy aimed at eradication for people with cystic fibrosis: whose airway secretions persistently test positive for non-tuberculous mycobacteria and who are clinically unwell with pulmonary disease, or who have a chest CT scan showing changes consistent with non-tuberculous mycobacteria disease and whose pulmonary disease has not responded to other recommended treatments. mcqs.question: Which drug is a NICE TA option for chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection in CF?
mcqs.explanation: Colistimethate sodium DPI is a TA option for chronic P. aeruginosa infection when continued colistimethate would be beneficial.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Colistimethate sodium DPI is recommended as an option in NICE technology appraisal guidance for treating chronic pulmonary infection caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa in people with cystic fibrosis only if they would clinically benefit from continued colistimethate sodium but do not tolerate it in its nebulised form, and thus tobramycin therapy would otherwise be considered. For full details, see the guidance on colistimethate sodium DPI (TA276, 2013) .

mcqs.question: Which of these is a NICE criterion for referring suspected CF to a specialist centre?
mcqs.explanation: Refer if the sweat test is positive or equivocal, assessment suggests CF despite normal tests, or gene testing finds 1 or more CF mutations.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Refer people with suspected cystic fibrosis to a specialist cystic fibrosis centre if: they have a positive or equivocal sweat test result; their assessment suggests they have cystic fibrosis but their test results are normal; gene testing reveals 1 or more cystic fibrosis mutations.

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest considering a DXA scan in CF?

options.C: Never, as DXA is unhelpful in CF
options.E: Only after a fracture has occurred

mcqs.explanation: Consider DXA for people at high risk of low bone mineral density, for example frequent oral steroids, frequent IV antibiotics, severe lung disease or undernutrition.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) bone density scans for people with cystic fibrosis who have factors that put them at high risk of low bone mineral density, such as: frequent or long-term oral corticosteroid use; frequent intravenous antibiotic use; severe lung disease; undernutrition; previous low-impact fractures; previous transplants; post menopause.

mcqs.question: How does NICE suggest separating patients with intermittent Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolation?
mcqs.explanation: Consider keeping these patients separate from those without the infection, for example with separate outpatient clinics.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider keeping people with cystic fibrosis who have intermittent isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa separate from people who do not have this infection, for example by using separate outpatient clinics. Help people with cystic fibrosis plan their inpatient attendance to avoid contact with each other, for example when they use: hospital restaurants, schools and recreation areas; diagnostic, treatment and pharmacy facilities (see information and support ).

mcqs.question: What does NICE recommend about CF clinic organisation to prevent cross-infection?

options.B: Run group education sessions for all

mcqs.explanation: Clinics should separate people individually, including how communal areas and facilities are used.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Each specialist cystic fibrosis clinic should be organised to prevent cross-infection. Separate people individually during the clinic, including by organising: the use of communal areas; attendance at diagnostic, treatment and pharmacy facilities.

mcqs.question: What does NICE say the specialist CF centre should provide for urgent enquiries?

options.D: A point of contact at all times

mcqs.correctAnswerText: A point of contact at all times
mcqs.explanation: The centre should have a point of contact available at all times, day or night, for urgent enquiries.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The specialist cystic fibrosis centre should have a point of contact available at all times (day or night) for urgent enquiries from people with cystic fibrosis and their family members or carers (as appropriate).

mcqs.question: What does NICE offer people with CF regarding exercise?

options.B: Fixed group classes for all patients

mcqs.explanation: Offer an individualised exercise programme that takes account of capability and preferences.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer people with cystic fibrosis an individualised exercise programme, taking into account their capability and preferences.

mcqs.question: Which of these is a NICE trigger for referring a person with CF to a liver specialist?

options.C: Any jaundice in the neonatal period

mcqs.explanation: Refer for chronic progressive liver disease (on clinical, blood or ultrasound assessment) or liver failure, among other criteria.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Refer people with cystic fibrosis to a liver specialist if they have any of the following: chronic progressive liver disease, based on clinical assessment, liver function blood tests or the findings on a liver ultrasound scan; liver failure, based on clinical assessment and liver function tests; portal hypertension, haematemesis, splenomegaly or findings on a liver ultrasound scan.

mcqs.question: A person with CF has no clinical evidence of lung disease. What does NICE recommend about airway clearance?
mcqs.explanation: Discuss airway clearance techniques, provide training and explain when to use them.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Discuss the use of airway clearance techniques with people with cystic fibrosis who do not have clinical evidence of lung disease and their parents or carers (as appropriate). Provide them with training in airway clearance techniques and explain when to use them.
